claim: The N-terminal domain (NTD) of SARS-CoV-2 that contains the RBD has lower homology to the corresponding subdomains of other CoVs than do the S2 subdomains.
source: the N-terminal domain (NTD) of SARS-CoV-2 that contains the RBD responsible for interacting with human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and initiating viral entry has lower homology to the corresponding subdomains of other CoVs than do the S2 subdomains where the fusion peptide, heptad repeat, and central helix required for fusion are located (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A and structural analysis described in the text

claim: Both the NTD and RBD of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein are poorly conserved across CoV.
source: structural comparison of various subdomains of the SARS-CoV-2 S protein shows that both the NTD and RBD of the spike protein are poorly conserved across CoV (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data presented in Figure 1B

claim: Superimposition of the SARS CoV-2 S1 and S2 domains with OC43 shows high structural conservation in S2 and the NTD, and a complete lack of homology in the RBD.
source: Superimposition of the SARS CoV-2 S1 and S2 domains with the most well-conserved widely circulating endemic human CoV, OC43, show high structural conservation in S2 and the NTD, and a complete lack of homology in the RBD that is consistent with the differing entry receptors used by these β-CoV (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural superimposition data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Preexisting antibodies raised against endemic human CoV are more likely to target the better-conserved regions of SARS-CoV-2 such as S2, and less likely to recognize the RBD.
source: Based on both structural and sequence homology, it stands to reason that preexisting antibodies raised against endemic human CoV are more likely to target the better-conserved regions of SARS-CoV-2 such as S2, and less likely to recognize the RBD (Yuan et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference based on structural and sequence homology data, supported by citations to prior work

claim: Elevated serum IgA and IgG but not IgM responses to whole S of diverse endemic CoV were frequently observed in SARS-CoV-2 convalescent subjects relative to naïve controls.
source: Relative to SARS-CoV-2-naïve controls, elevated serum IgA and IgG but not IgM responses to whole S of diverse endemic CoV were frequently observed (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Elevated levels of OC43-specific responses in serum were most pronounced among endemic CoV, but were largely restricted to the S2 domain and whole unstabilized S.
source: Among endemic CoV, elevated levels of OC43-specific responses in serum were most pronounced, but were largely restricted to the S2 domain and whole unstabilized S.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from serum analysis of convalescent subjects

claim: Elevated serum responses specific to the S1 domain of endemic CoV were not observed for any antibody isotype or subclass.
source: Indeed, elevated serum responses specific to the S1 domain of these CoV were not observed for any antibody isotype or subclass (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Elevated responses to endemic CoV were most pronounced for β-CoV (OC43 and HKU1) but were present for α-CoV as well in the JHMI convalescent cohort.
source: Elevated responses were most pronounced for β-CoV (OC43 and HKU1) but were present for α-CoV as well.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the JHMI convalescent cohort analysis

claim: The absence of elevated IgM responses among convalescent subjects is consistent with recall of class-switched antibodies as opposed to the de novo elicitation of cross-reactive antibodies.
source: The absence of elevated IgM responses among convalescent subjects is consistent with recall of class-switched antibodies as opposed to the de novo elicitation of cross-reactive antibodies.
evidence: Inference based on the observed pattern of antibody isotypes in convalescent subjects

claim: Elevated responses to OC43 S-2P among convalescent subjects in either cohort were not observed compared to naïve controls.
source: Whereas elevated responses to OC43 S-2P among convalescent subjects in either cohort were not observed compared to naïve controls, responses to both OC43 S and OC43 S2 (available only for the smaller cohort) were observed for IgG, but not IgM (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Elevation of endemic CoV antibody responses was also observed in nasopharyngeal wash samples and stool.
source: This effect was not limited to serum; elevation of endemic CoV antibody responses was also observed in nasopharyngeal wash samples (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and stool (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Elevated responses in mucosal samples were restricted to IgG and/or IgA isotypes, consistent with cross-reactive antibodies being boosted in a recall response during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Again, these elevated responses were restricted to IgG and/or IgA isotypes, consistent with cross-reactive antibodies being boosted in a recall response during SARS-CoV-2 infection, and were observed for whole S or the S2 domain, but not S1.
evidence: Inference based on the observed pattern of antibody isotypes in mucosal samples

claim: Acutely infected subjects had robustly elevated levels of CoV-2 unstabilized S-specific IgG compared to naïve controls at 2 weeks after a positive PCR diagnosis.
source: At this early timepoint, subjects appeared to have robustly elevated levels of CoV-2 unstabilized S-specific IgG compared to naïve controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: In acutely infected subjects, elevated responses to OC43 were observed for whole unstabilized S and the S2 domain, but not for the prefusion conformation-stabilized S-2P form of OC43 spike.
source: Again, these responses were observed for whole unstabilized S and the S2 domain, but not for the prefusion conformation-stabilized S-2P form of OC43 spike.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from acute infection cohort analysis

claim: Only a minor increase in IgM recognizing unstabilized OC43 S was observed (less than twofold) in acutely infected subjects.
source: In contrast, only a minor increase in IgM recognizing unstabilized OC43 S was observed (less than twofold) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The isotype profiles in acute infection suggest a recalled rather than novel response against the relevant cross-reactive epitopes in S2 and unstabilized spike.
source: Though cross-sectional in nature and reliant on a small number of subjects, these isotype profiles in acute infection nonetheless further suggest a recalled rather than novel response against the relevant cross-reactive epitopes in S2 and unstabilized spike, presumably in the postfusion conformation.
evidence: Inference based on the observed isotype profiles in acute infection cohort

claim: The median increase in OC43 S2-specific IgA and IgG were 3.7- and 20-fold, respectively, between the pre- and post-infection timepoints in the longitudinal cohort.
source: The median increase in OC43 S2-specific IgA and IgG were 3.7- and 20-fold, respectively, between the pre- and post-infection timepoints (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The median change in OC43 S2-specific IgM was within twofold between pre- and post-infection timepoints.
source: In contrast, the median change in OC43 S2-specific IgM was within twofold, providing further support that the elevated responses to endemic β-CoV are due to boosting of preexisting cross-reactive antibodies originally raised against homologous epitopes found in endemic CoV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from longitudinal cohort analysis

claim: Boosting of IgG responses specific to the full-length spike of HKU1 was observed following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Boosting of IgG responses specific to the full-length spike of another endemic β-CoV, HKU1, was also observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from longitudinal cohort analysis

claim: IgG and IgA but not IgM responses to whole unstabilized S, but not the S1 domain, of HKU1 were elevated following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: IgG and IgA but not IgM responses to whole unstabilized S, but not the S1 domain, of HKU1 were elevated following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Recalled cross-reactive antibodies may be more likely to recognize both the better-conserved S2 domain and post- rather than prefusion conformations of spike.
source: Collectively, these results further suggest that recalled cross-reactive antibodies may be more likely to recognize both the better-conserved S2 domain and post- rather than prefusion conformations of spike.
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of antibody responses to different spike conformations and domains

claim: The magnitude of IgG responses to CoV-2 S2 were well correlated to those binding unstabilized OC43 S (RP = 0.61).
source: Whereas the magnitude of IgG responses to CoV-2 S2 were well correlated to those binding unstabilized OC43 S (RP = 0.61) and its S2 domain (RP = 0.45), they were less well correlated to responses to stabilized OC43 S-2P (RP = 0.29) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 4A

claim: CoV-2-specific responses were better correlated to OC43 responses specific for unstabilized rather than stabilized spike.
source: CoV-2-specific responses were better correlated to OC43 responses specific for unstabilized rather than stabilized spike.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data

claim: IgG responses showed stronger correlative relationships with OC43 than did IgA, which were in turn stronger than IgM.
source: IgG responses showed stronger relationships than did IgA, which were in turn stronger than IgM.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data

claim: Among CoV-2 antigens tested, correlations with OC43 responses were strongest for the S2 domain and whole spike (S-2P), and weaker or absent for S1 and the RBD.
source: Lastly, among CoV-2 antigens tested, correlations with OC43 responses were strongest for the S2 domain and whole spike (S-2P), and weaker or absent for S1 and the RBD.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data

claim: The correlative relationships are consistent with recall of class-switched antibodies recognizing shared epitopes in the S2 domain from prior endemic CoV exposure induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Collectively, these correlative relationships are consistent with recall of class-switched antibodies recognizing shared epitopes in the S2 domain from prior endemic CoV exposure induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of correlative relationships observed

claim: OC43 S-specific fractions showed elevated recognition of CoV-2 S2 and S-2P, but not RBD.
source: For example, OC43 S-specific fractions showed elevated recognition of CoV-2 S2 and S-2P, but not RBD (Figure 5A), demonstrating molecular cross-reactivity as a general feature of polyclonal IgG responses in convalescent subjects.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data shown in Figure 5A

claim: IgG in the CoV-2 S2-specific fractions cross-reacted robustly with OC43 S, but no cross-reactivity in the IgM fraction was observed.
source: Additionally, IgG in the CoV-2 S2-specific fractions cross-reacted robustly with OC43 S, but no cross-reactivity in the IgM fraction was observed, despite a robust IgM response to CoV-2 S2 (Figure 5B), suggesting that while SARS-CoV-2 infection elicits IgM responses to the S2 domain, these presumed de novo responses are not cross-reactive to OC43.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Purified CoV-2 RBD and S-2P-specific fractions induced robust neutralization.
source: Whereas purified CoV-2 RBD and S-2P-specific fractions induced robust neutralization, neither purified OC43 S-specific nor SARS-CoV-2 S2 domain-specific serum antibodies had detectable neutralization activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Neither purified OC43 S-specific nor SARS-CoV-2 S2 domain-specific serum antibodies had detectable neutralization activity.
source: Whereas purified CoV-2 RBD and S-2P-specific fractions induced robust neutralization, neither purified OC43 S-specific nor SARS-CoV-2 S2 domain-specific serum antibodies had detectable neutralization activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: IgM, IgA, and IgG antibodies purified based on binding to SARS-CoV-2 RBD cross-reacted with proline-stabilized spike (S-2P and S-6P) and, to a lesser extent, unstabilized S, but showed no evidence of cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2 S2 or to endemic CoV.
source: IgM, IgA, and IgG antibodies purified based on binding to SARS-CoV-2 RBD cross-reacted with proline-stabilized spike (S-2P and S-6P) and, to a lesser extent, unstabilized S, but showed no evidence of cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2 S2 or to endemic CoV (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data shown in Figure 6A

claim: RBD-specific antibody responses raised by natural infection are unlikely to exhibit exceptionally broad CoV neutralization activity.
source: Because the overwhelming majority of neutralizing antibodies target the RBD, these results suggest that RBD-specific antibody responses raised by natural infection are unlikely to exhibit exceptionally broad CoV neutralization activity.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of cross-reactivity of RBD-specific antibodies to endemic CoV and established knowledge about neutralizing antibodies

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RBD-specific antibodies showed low, albeit detectable, cross-reactivity toward even SARS-CoV S and S1.
source: Indeed, SARS-CoV-2 RBD-specific antibodies showed low, albeit detectable, cross-reactivity toward even SARS-CoV S and S1.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data

claim: Both IgA and IgG components of SARS-CoV-2 S-2P-specific serum antibody fractions showed binding to OC43, but cross-reactive IgM was not evident.
source: However, while both IgA and IgG components of SARS-CoV-2 S-2P-specific serum antibody fractions showed binding to OC43, cross-reactive IgM was not evident.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data

claim: IgA and IgG, but not IgM, specific for SARS-CoV-2 S2 bound to SARS-CoV-2 proteins as well as OC43, SARS-CoV, MERS, and other endemic CoV S2 domains.
source: Similarly, IgA and IgG, but not IgM, specific for SARS-CoV-2 S2 bound as expected to SARS-CoV-2 proteins as well as OC43, SARS-CoV, MERS, and other endemic CoV S2 domains (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data shown in Figure 6C

claim: OC43 S-specific IgA and IgM fractions showed cross-reactivity to a broad array of endemic CoV S but not S1 proteins.
source: IgA and IgM fractions showed cross-reactivity to a broad array of endemic CoV S but not S1 proteins.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data

claim: OC43-specific IgA and IgG antibodies showed cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2 proteins containing the S2 domain.
source: Likewise, OC43-specific IgA and IgG antibodies showed cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2 proteins containing the S2 domain.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data

claim: OC43 S-specific IgM antibodies showed elevated recognition of diverse pandemic, pathogenic, and endemic S proteins in unstabilized forms, but a lack of recognition of stabilized prefusion conformations of CoV-2 spike, or the S1 domains of most other CoV tested.
source: In contrast, OC43 S-specific IgM antibodies showed elevated recognition of diverse pandemic, pathogenic, and endemic S proteins in unstabilized forms, but a lack of recognition of stabilized prefusion conformations of CoV-2 spike, or the S1 domains of most other CoV tested.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification and cross-reactivity testing data

claim: Immunization with stabilized spike (S-2P) failed to result in elevated IgG responses to endemic CoV among pregnant women, despite inducing considerably greater levels of SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies.
source: Fascinatingly, despite inducing considerably greater levels of SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies, immunization with stabilized spike (S-2P) failed to result in elevated IgG responses to endemic CoV among pregnant women (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing infected and vaccinated pregnant women shown in Figure 7

claim: Elevated levels of OC43-reactive IgA responses were not observed among vaccinated mothers.
source: Similarly, elevated levels of OC43-reactive IgA responses were not observed among vaccinated mothers, and neither infected nor vaccinated mothers showed elevated levels of OC43-reactive IgM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: In the validation cohort of mRNA-vaccinated healthy adults, while IgG responses to OC43 were statistically significantly elevated for S and S2 antigens, the effect was small (<2.5-fold).
source: In this cohort, while IgG responses to OC43 were statistically significantly elevated for S and S2 antigens, the effect was small (<2.5-fold) (Figure 7); elevated IgA or IgM responses were not observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from vaccinated healthy adults shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The differing immunogenicity profiles between natural infection and vaccination suggest that the presentation of native spike in the context of natural infection and stabilized spike in the context of mRNA vaccination are distinct.
source: These differing immunogenicity profiles suggest that the presentation of native spike in the context of natural infection and stabilized spike in the context of mRNA vaccination are distinct.
evidence: Inference based on the observed differences in antibody responses between infected and vaccinated subjects

claim: Elevated IgA and IgG but not IgM responses to the endemic CoV OC43 were observed in five distinct cohorts of naturally infected subjects.
source: In sum, elevated IgA and IgG but not IgM responses to the endemic CoV OC43 were observed in five distinct cohorts, including acutely infected, cross-sectional, and longitudinal convalescent cohorts.
evidence: Summary of experimental data across multiple cohorts

claim: Two cohorts of subjects immunized with stabilized spike in the form of mRNA-based vaccines showed no (IgA and IgM) or only a small (IgG only, and in only one cohort) elevation of binding to endemic CoV OC43.
source: In contrast, two cohorts of subjects immunized with stabilized spike in the form of mRNA-based vaccines showed no (IgA and IgM) or only a small (IgG only, and in only one cohort) elevation of binding to endemic CoV OC43 (Figure 8).
evidence: Summary of experimental data from vaccinated cohorts shown in Figure 8

claim: The lack of boosting of responses that cross-react with endemic CoV combined with high levels of neutralization activity from vaccination suggest favorable antigenicity of the prefusion conformation of S.
source: In combination with the lack of boosting of responses that cross-react with endemic CoV, the high levels of neutralization activity observed to result from vaccination (Jackson et al., 2020) suggest favorable antigenicity of the prefusion conformation of S, and that, if detrimental, the costs of original antigenic sin might be avoided by immunogen design.
evidence: Inference based on the observed differences between infection and vaccination, supported by citation to prior work on vaccine neutralization

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic represents the third time in just two decades that a novel coronavirus (CoV) with significant morbidity and mortality has begun to circulate among humans.
source: The ongoing pandemic of SARS-CoV-2 represents the third time in just two decades that a novel coronavirus (CoV) with significant morbidity and mortality has begun to circulate among humans (Peeri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has proven to be highly transmissible, infecting a substantial portion of the global population.
source: Unlike in the earlier outbreaks of SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, however, SARS-CoV-2 has proven to be highly transmissible, infecting a substantial portion of the global population – a conservative estimate of the prevalence of infection based on only confirmed cases corresponds to over 2% (COVID, 2021), while estimates of the total figure in the United States exceed 16% of the population (Reese et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to epidemiological data

claim: Under the hypothesis of original antigenic sin, preexisting humoral memory imprinted from prior exposure to related antigens partially predestines the antibody repertoire to focus on the epitopes of a new threat that closely resemble those for which there is an existing solution.
source: Under the hypothesis of original antigenic sin, preexisting humoral memory imprinted from prior exposure to related antigens partially predestines the antibody repertoire to focus on the epitopes of a new threat that closely resemble those for which there is an existing solution.
evidence: Description of the original antigenic sin hypothesis

claim: Original antigenic sin may hinder the immune system's ability to generate effective neutralizing antibodies because neutralizing epitopes are subject to additional selective pressure.
source: Because neutralizing epitopes are subject to additional selective pressure, this recall and re-diversification of existing antibody lineages may hinder the immune system's ability to generate effective neutralizing antibodies (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: Explanation of the mechanism of original antigenic sin, supported by citation

claim: Original antigenic sin has been most convincingly established in the context of influenza virus infection.
source: This phenomenon has been most convincingly established in the context of influenza virus infection, with support from both well-controlled animal model experiments (Kim et al., 2009; Nachbagauer et al., 2017) and observational studies of human natural infection histories (Francis et al., 1947; Fonville et al., 2014; Kucharski et al., 2015; Gostic et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on influenza

claim: Similar observations of original antigenic sin have been made in the context of diverse dengue virus serotypes.
source: Similar observations have been made in the context of diverse dengue virus serotypes (Midgley et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on dengue

claim: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) is a phenomenon by which cross-reactive antibodies induced by a prior exposure to a related pathogen promote infection of cell types bearing antibody Fc receptors and potentially elevate morbidity and mortality.
source: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), a phenomenon by which cross-reactive antibodies induced by a prior exposure to a related pathogen promote infection of cell types bearing antibody Fc receptors and potentially elevate morbidity and mortality (reviewed in Bournazos et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2015), suggests further potential advantages of a humoral blank slate.
evidence: Definition of ADE supported by citations to review articles

claim: ADE has been observed in vitro for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Though observed in vitro (Wu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), there has not been abundant evidence for the biological relevance of classical ADE in the context of SARS-CoV-2 in vivo (Li et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: There has not been abundant evidence for the biological relevance of classical ADE in the context of SARS-CoV-2 in vivo.
source: Though observed in vitro (Wu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), there has not been abundant evidence for the biological relevance of classical ADE in the context of SARS-CoV-2 in vivo (Li et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The role of non-neutralizing antibodies resulting from cross-strain challenges in promoting ADE in cases of dengue fever has motivated concern about COVID-19 enhancement.
source: Nonetheless, the role of non-neutralizing antibodies resulting from cross-strain challenges in promoting ADE in cases of dengue fever (Katzelnick et al., 2017) has motivated concern about COVID-19 enhancement (Lee et al., 2020; Fierz and Walz, 2020; Arvin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on dengue and COVID-19

claim: Studies have suggested that recent endemic CoV infection is associated with reduced severity of COVID-19.
source: The extent to which preexisting responses to prior endemic CoV exposures may influence responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination is not yet clear, but has been suggested from studies relating recent endemic CoV infection with reduced severity of COVID-19 (Sagar et al., 2021; Aran et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Numerous studies have observed elevated responses to endemic CoV following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Numerous studies have observed elevated responses to endemic CoV following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Guo et al., 2021; Morgenlander et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Kaplonek et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2021), and more recent work has shown that the magnitude of this 'back-boosting' effect is inversely correlated with the induction of IgG and IgM against SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein (Aydillo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: The magnitude of the 'back-boosting' effect to endemic CoV is inversely correlated with the induction of IgG and IgM against SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein.
source: Numerous studies have observed elevated responses to endemic CoV following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Guo et al., 2021; Morgenlander et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Kaplonek et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2021), and more recent work has shown that the magnitude of this 'back-boosting' effect is inversely correlated with the induction of IgG and IgM against SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein (Aydillo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Lower titers of neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 may result from boosting of preexisting cross-reactive lineages according to the original antigenic sin hypothesis.
source: Given differential degrees of homology between the receptor-binding domain (RBD) in S1 that is the target of the majority of neutralizing antibodies, and the better-conserved S2 domain that may be the target of antibodies with diverse effector functions but which are rarely neutralizing, the original antigenic sin hypothesis suggests that lower titers of neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 may result from boosting of preexisting cross-reactive lineages.
evidence: Inference based on the original antigenic sin hypothesis and structural differences between spike domains

claim: Antibody cross-reactivity between SARS-CoV-2 and endemic CoV has been observed for select monoclonal antibodies that have been cloned and cross-tested.
source: To date, antibody cross-reactivity has been inferred from indirect evidence in the form of boosted responses to endemic CoV (Guo et al., 2021; Morgenlander et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Kaplonek et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2021), and more conclusively observed for select monoclonal antibodies that have been cloned and cross-tested (Sakharkar et al., 2021; Dugan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on monoclonal antibodies

claim: Some studies of natural infection have suggested that boosted responses to endemic CoV are not associated with protection, but instead with more severe disease.
source: While some studies of natural infection have suggested that these boosted responses are not associated with protection, but instead with more severe disease (Guo et al., 2021; Aydillo et al., 2021; Dugan et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2022; Anderson et al., 2021; Gombar et al., 2021), others have supported the opposite conclusion (Aran et al., 2020; Dugas et al., 2021a; Dugas et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Some studies have supported the conclusion that boosted responses to endemic CoV are associated with protection.
source: While some studies of natural infection have suggested that these boosted responses are not associated with protection, but instead with more severe disease (Guo et al., 2021; Aydillo et al., 2021; Dugan et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2022; Anderson et al., 2021; Gombar et al., 2021), others have supported the opposite conclusion (Aran et al., 2020; Dugas et al., 2021a; Dugas et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Cross-reactive antibodies could interact with Fc receptors found on the surface of innate immune cells and promote protective effector function activities, including antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
source: Cross-reactive antibodies could interact with Fc receptors found on the surface of innate immune cells and promote protective effector function activities, including antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (Fox et al., 2019; Earnest et al., 2019; Clark, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on antibody effector functions

claim: A subset of monoclonal antibodies isolated from SARS-CoV patients that were able to cross-react with, but not neutralize, SARS-CoV-2 were able to confer protection or reduce viral spread in mouse models.
source: To this end, a subset of monoclonal antibodies isolated from SARS-CoV patients that were able to cross-react with, but not neutralize, SARS-CoV-2 were able to confer protection or reduce viral spread in mouse models (Shiakolas et al., 2021; Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on monoclonal antibodies in mouse models

claim: Passive transfer experiments of monoclonal antibodies have shown that effector mechanisms contribute to antiviral activity in vivo.
source: Indeed, both passive transfer experiments of monoclonal antibodies (Atyeo et al., 2021; Suryadevara et al., 2021; Tortorici et al., 2020; Winkler et al., 2021; Chan et al., 2021; Schäfer et al., 2021) and evaluation of polyclonal antibodies raised in the context of vaccination or infection (Alter et al., 2021; Francica et al., 2021; Adeniji et al., 2021) have shown that effector mechanisms contribute to antiviral activity in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Evaluation of polyclonal antibodies raised in the context of vaccination or infection have shown that effector mechanisms contribute to antiviral activity in vivo.
source: Indeed, both passive transfer experiments of monoclonal antibodies (Atyeo et al., 2021; Suryadevara et al., 2021; Tortorici et al., 2020; Winkler et al., 2021; Chan et al., 2021; Schäfer et al., 2021) and evaluation of polyclonal antibodies raised in the context of vaccination or infection (Alter et al., 2021; Francica et al., 2021; Adeniji et al., 2021) have shown that effector mechanisms contribute to antiviral activity in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Evidence of in vivo contributions of antibody effector mechanisms extends to mechanistic evidence via Fc sequence engineering to knock out or enhance these activities.
source: This evidence extends beyond correlative observations (Tortorici et al., 2020; Alter et al., 2021) to include mechanistic (Peeri et al., 2020) evidence of in vivo contributions via Fc sequence engineering to knock out or enhance these activities (Suryadevara et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2021; Yamin et al., 2021), as well as on the basis of depletion of effector cells (Winkler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on Fc engineering and effector cell depletion

claim: This study provides evidence that antibodies targeting OC43 are robustly boosted in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection but not vaccination with stabilized S.
source: In sum, this study provides evidence that antibodies targeting OC43 are robustly boosted in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection but not vaccination with stabilized S, and that the S2 subdomain of the spike protein is likely responsible for triggering a recalled, IgG-dominated response (Figure 9).
evidence: Summary of the study's main findings, supported by data presented throughout and illustrated in Figure 9

claim: The S2 subdomain of the spike protein is likely responsible for triggering a recalled, IgG-dominated response.
source: In sum, this study provides evidence that antibodies targeting OC43 are robustly boosted in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection but not vaccination with stabilized S, and that the S2 subdomain of the spike protein is likely responsible for triggering a recalled, IgG-dominated response (Figure 9).
evidence: Summary of the study's main findings, supported by data presented throughout and illustrated in Figure 9

claim: The recalled, cross-reactive response to endemic CoV is non-neutralizing.
source: While non-neutralizing, the role of these cross-reactive antibodies in the context of infection is not yet known.
evidence: Supported by neutralization assay data presented in the study

claim: The differing antigenicity of natural infection and vaccination with stabilized prefusion spike has potential implications for the breadth and level of protection afforded by each.
source: While other antiviral activities of broadly cross-reactive S2-specifc antibodies are not known, the differing antigenicity of natural infection and vaccination with stabilized prefusion spike has potential implications for the breadth and level of protection afforded by each.
evidence: Inference based on the observed differences in antibody responses between infection and vaccination
